questions.subject: math
questions.syllabusRef: M-2 / Functions and Sequences / Exponential and Logarithmic Functions / Power and quadratic functions
questions.solution:
Complete the square. Halve the coefficient of $x$ to get $-3$, then square it:
$$x^{2}-6x+11=(x-3)^{2}-9+11=(x-3)^{2}+2.$$

A square is never negative, so $(x-3)^{2}\ge 0$, and the smallest it can be is $0$ at $x=3$. At that point
$$y_{\min}=0+2=2.$$
distractorRationale: Correct. Completing the square gives $(x-3)^{2}+2$, so the least value is $2$, reached at $x=3$.
This is $x=3$, the input where the minimum happens, not the minimum value itself.
This is the $9$ produced while completing the square. It has to be subtracted again, not reported as the answer.
This is $y$ at $x=0$, the intercept on the vertical axis. The curve dips well below it before turning.

questions.subject: math
questions.syllabusRef: M-2 / Functions and Sequences / Exponential and Logarithmic Functions / Power and quadratic functions
questions.stem: Which of the following is a power function?
questions.solution:
A power function has the variable in the **base** and a constant in the exponent:
$$y=x^{a}, \qquad a \text{ constant}.$$

Check each candidate against that shape. Only $y=x^{\frac{1}{2}}$ has $x$ as the base with a fixed exponent, so it is the power function. (It is the square root function, written another way.)
distractorRationale: This is an exponential function: the variable is in the exponent and the base is fixed. That is the opposite arrangement.
Correct. The variable is the base and the exponent $\tfrac{1}{2}$ is a constant, which is exactly the form $y=x^{a}$.
This is a logarithmic function, the inverse of an exponential one. It is not of the form $y=x^{a}$.
This is linear. It can be written $y=2x^{1}+1$, but the extra $+1$ means it is not a single power of $x$.

verification.justification: A power function is by definition y = x^a with the variable as the base and a constant exponent. Only option B has that form; A is exponential, C is logarithmic, and D is linear with a constant term added.

questions.subject: math
questions.syllabusRef: M-2 / Functions and Sequences / Exponential and Logarithmic Functions / Power and quadratic functions
questions.stem: The parabola $y=x^{2}+bx+9$ meets the horizontal axis at exactly one point. Given that $b>0$, the value of $b$ is
questions.solution:
"Meets the axis at exactly one point" means the equation $x^{2}+bx+9=0$ has a repeated root, which happens exactly when the discriminant is zero:
$$\Delta=b^{2}-4ac=0.$$

Here $a=1$ and $c=9$, so
$$b^{2}-4(1)(9)=0 \ \Longrightarrow\ b^{2}=36 \ \Longrightarrow\ b=\pm 6.$$

The question asks for the positive value, so $b=6$. (Check: $x^{2}+6x+9=(x+3)^{2}$, which touches the axis at $x=-3$ and nowhere else.)
distractorRationale: Solved $b^{2}=9$ instead of $b^{2}=36$, which drops the factor of $4a$ from the discriminant.
Set $b$ equal to the constant term. The constant is $c$; $b$ is the coefficient of $x$ and is found from the discriminant.
Correct. $\Delta=b^{2}-36=0$ gives $b=6$ for the positive root, and $x^{2}+6x+9=(x+3)^{2}$.
Used $\Delta=b^{2}-4ac$ with $c$ doubled somewhere, giving $b^{2}=144$. The constant term is $9$, not $36$.

questions.subject: math
questions.syllabusRef: M-2 / Functions and Sequences / Exponential and Logarithmic Functions / Exponential functions and their graphs
questions.stem: For every $a>0$ with $a \neq 1$, the graph of $y=a^{x}$ passes through which fixed point?
questions.solution:
A point is fixed only if it works for **every** allowed $a$. So look for an input whose output does not depend on $a$.

Put $x=0$:
$$y=a^{0}=1 \qquad \text{for every } a>0.$$

So every such graph passes through $(0,\ 1)$, whatever the base.

Any other input does depend on $a$. At $x=1$, for instance, $y=a$, which is $2$ for $a=2$ and $3$ for $a=3$ — a moving point, not a fixed one.
distractorRationale: Would need $a^{0}=0$, but any non-zero number raised to the power $0$ is $1$. An exponential graph never touches the horizontal axis.
Would need $a^{1}=0$, which is impossible for $a>0$.
Only true for the single base $a=1$, and that base is excluded. For any other base, $a^{1}=a \neq 1$.
Correct. $a^{0}=1$ for every allowed base, so $(0,\ 1)$ lies on all of these graphs.

verification.justification: A fixed point must satisfy y = a^x for all admissible a. Since a^0 = 1 for every a > 0, the point (0, 1) qualifies. At x = 1 the value is a itself, which varies, so no point with x = 1 is fixed; and a^x is strictly positive, so no point with y = 0 is on the graph.

questions.subject: math
questions.syllabusRef: M-2 / Functions and Sequences / Exponential and Logarithmic Functions / Exponential functions and their graphs
questions.solution:
Write both sides as powers of the same base. Since $27=3^{3}$:
$$3^{2x-1}=3^{3}.$$

An exponential function takes each value only once, so the exponents must match:
$$2x-1=3 \ \Longrightarrow\ 2x=4 \ \Longrightarrow\ x=2.$$

Check: $3^{2(2)-1}=3^{3}=27$.
distractorRationale: Correct. Matching exponents gives $2x-1=3$, so $x=2$.
Set $2x-1=1$, matching against $3^{1}$ rather than $3^{3}$.
Stopped at the exponent itself, $2x-1=3$, and reported the right-hand side instead of solving for $x$.
Solved $2x-1=3$ but added rather than divided: $x=3+2$.

questions.subject: math
questions.syllabusRef: M-2 / Functions and Sequences / Exponential and Logarithmic Functions / Exponential functions and their graphs
questions.stem: Which of the following functions is decreasing on the whole of $\mathbb{R}$?
questions.solution:
For $y=a^{x}$ the direction is decided entirely by the base:
$$a>1 \Rightarrow \text{increasing}, \qquad 0<a<1 \Rightarrow \text{decreasing}.$$

Check the two exponentials. Base $3$ is greater than $1$, so $y=3^{x}$ increases. Base $\tfrac{1}{4}$ lies between $0$ and $1$, so $y=\left(\tfrac{1}{4}\right)^{x}$ decreases everywhere.

The other two are not exponentials at all. $y=x^{3}$ increases throughout, and $y=x^{2}+1$ falls then rises, so neither is decreasing on all of $\mathbb{R}$.
distractorRationale: Base $3>1$, so this increases. Larger $x$ gives a larger power.
Correct. The base $\tfrac{1}{4}$ lies strictly between $0$ and $1$, so raising it to larger powers gives smaller values.
A cubic with a positive coefficient, which increases across the whole line rather than decreasing.
Decreasing on $(-\infty,\ 0]$ but increasing on $[0,\ +\infty)$, so it is not decreasing on all of $\mathbb{R}$.

questions.subject: math
questions.syllabusRef: M-2 / Functions and Sequences / Exponential and Logarithmic Functions / Exponential functions and their graphs
questions.stem: The equation $9^{x}-4\cdot 3^{x}+3=0$ has two real solutions. Their sum is
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — spot the hidden quadratic.** Note that $9^{x}=(3^{2})^{x}=(3^{x})^{2}$. Substituting $t=3^{x}$ turns the equation into
$$t^{2}-4t+3=0.$$

**Step 2 — solve for $t$.** Factorising,
$$(t-1)(t-3)=0 \ \Longrightarrow\ t=1 \ \text{ or } \ t=3.$$
Both are positive, so both give a genuine value of $x$. (A negative or zero $t$ would have to be discarded, since $3^{x}>0$ always.)

**Step 3 — go back to $x$.**
$$3^{x}=1 \Rightarrow x=0, \qquad 3^{x}=3 \Rightarrow x=1.$$

The sum is $0+1=1$.
distractorRationale: Found only the root $x=0$, from $t=1$, and missed the second value of $t$.
Added the two values of $t$ instead of the two values of $x$: $1+3=4$. The substitution has to be undone before summing.
Correct. $t=3^{x}$ gives $t=1$ or $t=3$, hence $x=0$ or $x=1$, and $0+1=1$.
Reported the larger value of $t$ rather than a value of $x$ at all.

questions.subject: math
questions.syllabusRef: M-2 / Functions and Sequences / Exponential and Logarithmic Functions / Logarithms and logarithmic functions
questions.solution:
A logarithm asks: to what power must the base be raised to reach the number?

Here the base is $5$ and the number is $125$. Since
$$5^{3}=125,$$
the answer is $3$.
distractorRationale: The reciprocal of the answer. This would be $\log_{125}5$, with the base and the number swapped.
The base itself, not the exponent the base has to be raised to.
This is $5^{2}$. Two fives are not enough — $125$ needs three.

questions.subject: math
questions.syllabusRef: M-2 / Functions and Sequences / Exponential and Logarithmic Functions / Logarithms and logarithmic functions
questions.solution:
Two logarithms with the same base subtract into the logarithm of a quotient:
$$\log_{2}6-\log_{2}3=\log_{2}\!\left(\frac{6}{3}\right)=\log_{2}2.$$

And $2^{1}=2$, so $\log_{2}2=1$.
distractorRationale: Correct. The difference of logarithms is the logarithm of the quotient: $\log_{2}(6/3)=\log_{2}2=1$.
Divided the two logarithms rather than subtracting them, and then mis-evaluated the result.
Subtracted the *numbers* to get $\log_{2}3$ from $6-3$. The rule applies to the logarithms, turning subtraction into division.
Divided $6$ by $3$ correctly but then reported $6/2$, or confused the quotient with the base.

questions.subject: math
questions.syllabusRef: M-2 / Functions and Sequences / Exponential and Logarithmic Functions / Logarithms and logarithmic functions
questions.solution:
A logarithm is defined only for a strictly positive argument, so the requirement is
$$2x-6>0.$$

Solve it:
$$2x>6 \ \Longrightarrow\ x>3.$$

The inequality is strict, so $x=3$ is excluded — at that point the argument is $0$, and $\log_{3}0$ does not exist.
$$\text{Domain}=(3,\ +\infty).$$
distractorRationale: Required $x>0$, as if the argument of the logarithm were $x$ itself rather than $2x-6$.
Correct. $2x-6>0$ gives $x>3$, with $3$ excluded because the argument would be $0$ there.
Included $x=3$. At that value the argument is exactly $0$, and the logarithm of $0$ is undefined.
Reversed the inequality. For $x<3$ the argument $2x-6$ is negative, where the logarithm is also undefined.

questions.subject: math
questions.syllabusRef: M-2 / Functions and Sequences / Exponential and Logarithmic Functions / Logarithms and logarithmic functions
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — factorise the number.** Break $18$ into the primes whose logarithms are given:
$$18=2 \times 9=2 \times 3^{2}.$$

**Step 2 — split the logarithm.** A product becomes a sum, and a power becomes a multiplier:
$$\log_{a}18=\log_{a}2+\log_{a}3^{2}=\log_{a}2+2\log_{a}3.$$

**Step 3 — substitute.**
$$\log_{a}18=m+2n.$$

The pattern to remember: the exponent inside comes out as a *coefficient*, never as a power of the answer.
distractorRationale: Attached the $2$ to the wrong factor, as though $18=2^{2}\times 3$. In fact $18=2\times 3^{2}$.
Turned the product into a product of logarithms. $\log(xy)$ is $\log x+\log y$, not $\log x \cdot \log y$.
Correct. $18=2\times 3^{2}$, so $\log_{a}18=\log_{a}2+2\log_{a}3=m+2n$.
Brought the exponent down as a power of $n$ instead of a coefficient. $\log_{a}3^{2}=2\log_{a}3$, not $(\log_{a}3)^{2}$.
